answer: The observation that transfers is that the people who actually decide a cement purchase are the mason and contractor on site, not the homeowner reading the ad. So the work has to speak in their language and about their concerns, strength and reliability, in a simple, earthy, local idiom. Pandey turns the episode into a lesson about gut feel, passion and 'thinking Indian'. That lesson is a personal credo. The transferable point is narrower: find the real influencer in the buying chain and brief to that person. [unsure]

The calibration fixed level noise, the differences in each reviewer's average severity, for those two reviewers. It did not touch pattern noise, which is each judge's idiosyncratic response to particular cases (stable pattern noise), or occasion noise, which is the same judge varying with mood, time or order. System noise is level noise plus pattern noise, and in the book's audits pattern noise is usually the larger part. It also leaves shared bias alone. A noise audit would have revealed the rest: all five reviewers independently judge the same set of cases, with repeats where possible, and you measure the variability case by case, not only the averages.

The five steps are: (1) narrow the focus, (2) stock in depth, (3) buy cheap, (4) sell cheap, (5) dominate the category. Step 1 is contraction, which the Law of Contraction praises. Step 2, however, means carrying a huge assortment within the category, so the brand's promise becomes breadth and selection. Step 5, domination, rewards growth, and a dominant retailer comes under pressure to widen the category it dominates. Both pull toward the expansion the book condemns elsewhere. The book never says where 'deep' becomes 'broad', or when domination turns into line extension.

Airey's line is that the client pays for your expertise, not for a pair of hands. Feedback should be judged against the brief and the business objectives, not personal taste, and the number of rounds should be limited. If the boundary is not held, the job turns into design by committee: endless revisions and a watered-down compromise mark nobody chose, and the designer ends up as a software operator. To make it concrete he advises writing the scope into the contract, for example a fixed number of concepts and revision rounds, with more charged extra. [unsure]

SC 1.4.5 Images of Text (Level AA) applies only 'if the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation'. In that case text must be used instead of images of text, with two exceptions. Customizable: the image of text can be visually customized to the user's requirements. Essential: a particular presentation is essential, such as logotypes. SC 1.4.9 Images of Text (No Exception) (Level AAA) drops the technology condition and the customizable exception. Images of text are allowed only for pure decoration or where the particular presentation is essential, and logotypes still count as essential.

Hopkins says a guarantee's power lies in the confidence it signals, the maker's visible willingness to take the risk himself, not in the legal or money-back terms, which few people ever invoke. The second effect he reports is on the advertiser's side. Claims under the guarantee turned out to be rare, and offering it made dealers and the maker's own organisation more confident, and more careful about the product. Neither effect follows from the wording of the terms. It is the psychology of the offer that sells. [unsure]

The reason given is attention: bright, high-contrast visuals stand out and hook viewers in a fast-scrolling feed, often on small mobile screens and sometimes with the sound off, so the ad registers in the first seconds. The guidance does not supply thresholds, meaning no contrast ratio, brightness or saturation value, and no definition of 'bright'. It also gives no causal evidence isolating this factor from the other ABCD elements, and no guidance on when brightness conflicts with brand palettes or mood. It is a heuristic, not a measurable specification.

Hopkins says charging for a sample, even ten cents, cuts replies sharply, by about three-quarters in his experience. Collecting and handling the coins can cost more than the samples saved, and the enquirers you lose include many good prospects, so the cost per real customer rises. His view is that it is better to give samples freely but only to people who have read the ad and asked for them. On half-price offers, a reduced-price offer does not create a true trial and cheapens the product in the buyer's mind. People who buy at half price act on a bargain, not on conviction about the product. [unsure]

If the mark will live mainly on cheap printed leaflets handed out at events, it has to reproduce reliably: small, possibly in one or two colours, on low-grade paper and photocopies, and readable at a glance in a busy hall. So you need simple forms, no fine detail or gradients, and a version that works in black and white. Airey's point is that the brief comes first. Before designing, ask where and how the logo will be used, how the client currently promotes itself, and what the budget and reproduction methods are.

Freeman treats the implied connection as the whole point of juxtaposition. Two elements that have no real relationship are brought together by viewpoint and timing, and the viewer supplies the link. The meaning is created by the photographer and completed by the viewer, often as irony or wit. It is not a claim of fact that either person meant anything. For him it is a legitimate graphic and narrative device, the photographer's comment built from framing, and dishonesty is not the relevant category. The relationship is openly one of image construction. [unsure]

Phase one is fast and uncritical. You pour out the obvious ideas, clichés and first thoughts to get them out of your head, looking for the territory and the basic truth or benefit so the easy answers are cleared away. Phase two pushes past them to unexpected, fresh angles and executions. When phase two stalls and nothing surprising comes, Sullivan reverses. He goes back to the simple, straight statement of the product's benefit and makes that plain truth interesting, since a simple truth well said beats a forced clever idea. [unsure]

Carroll tells photographers to stop concentrating only on the obvious subject and think about the viewer's experience. Give the viewer something to work out: leave space for questions and ambiguity, and hint rather than explain everything. The mechanism is engagement. When a picture withholds some information, the viewer's imagination fills the gaps, so they keep looking and become invested, while a picture that explains itself fully is consumed at once and dropped. [unsure]

No. The Understanding document for 1.4.11 says hover indicators are not in scope: a hover highlight is not visual information required to identify a component or its state. Contrast applies to states such as focus, checked, selected and pressed where they are shown visually, and to component boundaries only if those are what identify the component. A button does not need a visible border or boundary. If the text label identifies it (and meets text contrast), a borderless button passes. If a boundary or fill is the only thing identifying the button, it needs 3:1 against adjacent colours.

Freeman's answer was to change the viewpoint rather than the lens. He got up high, shooting from an elevated or aerial position (from the air), so the lighthouse could be read against the island, the shoreline and the surrounding sea at the same time. From that height the foreground no longer swamps the structure and the setting spreads out around it as a map-like context. The subject stays recognisable while the environment carries the story. [unsure]

Under the Law of Change, a brand can be changed: (1) when it is weak or does not exist in the mind, (2) when you want to move the brand down the food chain, and (3) when the brand is in a slow-moving field and the change happens over an extended period. The mechanism for the third is gradualism. Perception is shifted in small steps over years, so the prospect never sees a jolt, as with Marlboro's move from a women's cigarette to a cowboy brand. In a fast-moving field, the category and competitors move faster than perceptions can be moved, so the brand cannot reposition slowly enough to be believed.

The two errors are placing the subject only slightly off-centre, so it looks neither centred nor intentionally offset and reads as a mistake, and pushing it too far toward the edge, where it feels cramped or about to fall out of the frame. Because the errors sit on either side of the thirds lines, Carroll is not treating the rule of thirds as exact coordinates. He treats it as a target zone and a signal of intent. Off-centre placement has to be clearly deliberate and still balanced within the frame. [unsure]

Google's core table states: Attract: hook and sustain attention with an immersive story. Brand: integrate the brand early, richly and often (help viewers see and hear the brand). Connect: help people think or feel something. Direct: ask them to take action. Each line comes with supporting tactics, such as a tight opening frame, brand in the first five seconds, humanising the story and a clear call to action, but the one-line principles above are the gist. [unsure of exact wording]

Noise applies to professional judgments where variability is unwanted, that is, where interchangeable judges should ideally reach the same answer: sentencing, underwriting, diagnosis. It does not apply to matters of taste, where disagreement is expected and even valued (preferring a film or a flavour), or to creative and competitive settings where diversity of opinion is useful, such as generating options or some market bets. The test is whether you would want, and expect, different competent judges to agree, and whether a disagreement between them is a problem. If variability is harmless or desirable, it is not noise.

Parameswaran records cases where advertising did not mirror society. Some ads ran ahead of social reality, showing aspirational, liberated or Westernised portrayals most Indians did not live. Others lagged, keeping stereotyped gender roles long after attitudes had shifted, or were rejected by the public. Such a case matters more than the supporting ones because confirming examples are easy to pick after the fact. A disconfirming case shows advertising is a selective, commercially motivated representation, not a neutral record, and it limits how far ads can be used as historical evidence. [unsure]

For Sontag the photograph has no fixed meaning of its own. It takes the meaning given by its caption and its context of use. When a second party republishes it with their own caption, the image changes its meaning and can serve the opposite cause from the one intended. Captions, in her phrase, supply the missing voice. What the case establishes is that photographs are ambiguous and meaning depends on use. It does not establish that photographs are false or lack a real referent, or that every reading is equally valid. The trace of the real persists, but its interpretation is up for grabs. [unsure]

'Make the private public' belongs to the Public principle. For behaviour you want to spread, make it visible, through products that advertise themselves and behavioural residue (Movember, Livestrong bands, Apple's white earbuds), because people imitate what they can see others doing. 'Make the public private' applies when you want to stop a behaviour. Publicising how common an undesirable behaviour is (anti-drug ads) signals that it is normal, so you should hide it and highlight the desired behaviour instead. What he leaves unsaid is how to tell which case you are in when a behaviour is mixed, and how to make a behaviour visible without also normalising its non-adoption.

Ogilvy treats posters (billboards) sceptically. They are glanced at from moving traffic, can carry only a few words, he dislikes them as landscape pollution, and he admits little evidence on how well they sell. Subway cards he treats more favourably, as a medium read by a captive, idle audience that has minutes to fill, so longer copy can work there. Taken together, the subway case shows he judges a format by the reading situation, meaning how much attention and time the audience has, not by its prestige or reach alone. [unsure]

Connor and Irizarry treat silence as unexpressed feedback, not agreement. Someone quiet during critique may hold concerns or insights that come out later as objections, rework or passive resistance once decisions are made, and the facilitator wrongly reads silence as consensus. The pattern is the silent or withdrawn participant, often caused by status differences, dominant talkers or discomfort with the format. The remedy is to invite input directly and create structured turns. The limit is that you should not force people or put them on the spot. Draw them in without pressuring them. [unsure]

From the mid-1970s Indian advertising was increasingly written by Indians for Indians instead of by expatriate British staff. More important, copy began to be conceived originally in Hindi and regional languages rather than written in English and translated. The precise distinction is between translation (English ideas rendered into Hindi, with borrowed idiom) and original writing in the Indian language (ideas born in the vernacular, drawing on local idiom, humour and culture). This change gave rise to distinctly Indian advertising. [unsure]

Sullivan's rebuttal is that an ad which tries to say everything says nothing. The reader takes away at most one thing, and a crowded list gets ignored. He illustrates it with throwing several tennis balls at someone at once: they catch none, but throw one and they catch it. His reason is that attention is scarce and single-minded messages are remembered. When no argument persuades the client, his fallback is to find the single thread running through the range and make that the one idea, or to do the job as well as possible and save your fights for work that matters. [unsure]

Sontag says the photograph's meaning has changed each time, because a photograph's meaning depends on its context and use. It is not fixed in the image. The same picture reads as a work draft on the contact sheet, art in the gallery, evidence in the police file, propaganda at the demonstration, news in the magazine and a keepsake on the wall. She borrows Wittgenstein's formula for words, that the meaning is the use, and applies it to photographs.

Sullivan's diagnosis is that the problem is the headline, or the concept, not the body copy. If the copy has to explain what the headline meant, the headline failed and the idea is not clear on its own. Don't explain the joke. His prescription is to go back and fix the headline and visual so they communicate by themselves. The body copy should then pick up where the headline leaves off, continuing the conversation and supplying the reasons to believe, not decoding the idea.

Splicing and shifting keep the grid's orthogonal logic. Modules are cut, overlapped or slid, but they stay on horizontal and vertical axes. Non-orthogonal deconstruction rotates parts of the structure off the right angle, so elements sit on diagonals or several angled axes. Samara says this creates a sense of spatial depth and movement: angled planes seem to tilt, recede or advance, adding an illusion of three dimensions and dynamic tension. The effect is stronger when the angled elements are set against remaining orthogonal elements or the format edge, since the contrast with the rectilinear frame heightens it. [unsure]

Hopkins reasons from his agency's ledger. Most new ventures fail. If an agency took the full budget and the campaign failed, the client was ruined or left, and the agency lost the account, its future commissions and its reputation. A small test risks only a few thousand dollars in a few towns. Winners roll out nationally and pay commissions for years, while losers cost both sides little. So the arithmetic says the rule is not only protection for the client. It also protects the agency's income stream, reputation and record of successes. [unsure]

Sullivan's claim is that an exclamation point is a confession: the writer is trying to add excitement with punctuation because the words lack it, and readers sense the forced enthusiasm and trust the line less. It is like laughing at your own joke. He demonstrates by showing that a line either carries excitement on its own or it doesn't. Take the exclamation point off a strong line and nothing is lost. Add it to a weak line and the line only sounds more like a pushy ad. [unsure]

WCAG's test is that text is purely decorative if the words can be rearranged or substituted without changing their purpose. It is stricter than it looks. Most text that seems ornamental still carries meaning: brand names, headings, labels, even decorative quotations whose particular words matter. If swapping or scrambling the words would change anything the user needs, it is not decorative. Very little real text qualifies, so the exemption is narrow, and images of text used 'for look' usually still need text equivalents and must follow 1.4.5 or 1.4.9.

'Mother pious lady' is stock phrasing from Indian newspaper matrimonial ads, describing a prospective bride's or groom's mother as religious and virtuous. It signals the family's respectability, values and traditional grounding in a compressed, slightly odd Indian English. It suits Santosh Desai's book because the book reads middle-class Indian culture through small everyday artefacts and habits. One throwaway phrase carries a whole world of social codes: family, marriage, status and the blend of tradition and modernity. The small detail becomes a key to the larger culture.

In calendar and bazaar prints, a convention formed under early printing and commissioning limits. Images were composed for chromolithographic and early offset processes, with flat, saturated colour areas, frontal figures and a lower band or border left for the sponsoring firm's name, because the prints were given away as advertising calendars. When the constraint lapsed (better printing, and prints sold as devotional images with no sponsor), the conventions persisted. Artists and publishers kept the look because buyers now expected it as the proper look of a sacred image. The form carried on as style after its functional reason had gone. [unsure]

Hopkins says his agency turned down the great majority of propositions, roughly nine in ten, after a short investigation or test showed they could not succeed. He observes that the people who hesitate and want proof are usually the sound advertisers, while those most eager to spend are usually the weakest prospects. The reason he gives for refusing is not ethics or protecting clients' money. It is protecting the agency: failures damage its reputation and its record, and success stories are what bring new business. [unsure]

Samara repeatedly reports that layouts which look spontaneous, intuitive or 'ungridded' were built on careful underlying structure, deliberate proportional systems and many rounds of sketching and refinement. The ease is manufactured. This matters because appearance is poor evidence of process. You cannot infer from a finished, loose-looking layout that it was made freely, nor that rules were abandoned. When judging or imitating work you did not see being made, look for the hidden structure and do not copy only the surface informality.

'Jump in' means starting the story immediately, opening with action, product or people instead of a slow build-up. That is a property of time and narrative: how quickly something meaningful happens, pacing, motion and when the story begins across the first seconds. A single frame cannot show whether the action has started or whether the opening is a slow fade or logo card. It has to be judged on a sequence, with shot changes, motion and audio. The source does not give an operational definition: no time threshold, no measurable criteria for 'action', and no validation data for building a pass/fail rule.

Inside the book the 'laws' are qualified. (1) The Law of Change says brands can and sometimes should be changed, which contradicts immutability. (2) The authors admit exceptions and concede that brands breaking the laws sometimes succeed, attributing that to weak competition. (3) They present the laws as observations drawn from marketplace cases, a matter of perception and judgment, not as tested rules. These concessions reduce the overclaim in the title. They do not fix the method: the evidence is still selected anecdotes, hindsight explanation and survivorship, with no systematic testing, so 'immutable law' earns no extra weight. [unsure]

Sullivan says early easy ideas are a warning sign, not success. The first ideas to arrive are the obvious ones, the same ones any other team, and the client, would think of: clichés and category conventions. His instruction is to write them all down to get them out of your system, not fall in love with them, and keep going well past that point. The original ideas come after the easy ones run out, when the work gets hard.

The example is the Farm Security Administration photographers of the 1930s, who took dozens of frontal pictures of a sharecropper until they had the expression they wanted, one that matched their idea of poverty, dignity and so on. The point is that documentary photography is not neutral recording. It is selection and construction guided by the photographer's taste and ideology. On indiscriminate photographers, Sontag argues that photography's leveling tendency, treating everything as worth photographing, is itself a stance. It turns the world into a collection of equally interesting items and aestheticises it. Even indiscriminate shooting imposes a point of view. [unsure]

The source separates products by the role children play. For children's products such as breakfast cereal, children are the users and decisive influencers. For shared household goods such as soap, their influence is moderate, around brand or variant choice. For big-ticket family purchases such as a car, it is limited and indirect, voiced but not decisive, with parents deciding. The durable part is the distinction between user, influencer and decider/buyer, and the finding that influence varies with product category and price, not the particular percentages, which date. [unsure]

Pandey describes focus groups and research respondents saying what sounds socially correct or rational in front of others, not what they actually feel or do. Group dynamics, social desirability and a dominant voice distort the answers, so work that tests badly succeeds in market, or the reverse. The mechanism, people misreporting under social observation, is well supported in general. His evidence for the conclusion (trust instinct over research) is a few memorable anecdotes of ads that tested poorly and won, which are selectively recalled, lack counter-cases, and do not show that intuition beats better-designed research. [unsure]

Samara says structural intervals need not come from a column grid. They can be derived from the content and from proportion systems. He lists the proportions of the format itself, mathematical and natural ratios (the golden section, Fibonacci series, root rectangles), musical intervals and rhythms, the dimensions of images or other fixed elements, and typographic measures such as type size, leading and baseline increments. The structure then comes from an internal logic of relationships, not from equal columns. [unsure]

Airey makes the point that a logo does not have to show what the company does. BMW's mark shows no car, and a dentist's logo need not show a tooth. An element can be perfectly relevant, such as a tooth for a dentist or a house for an estate agent, and still be wrong. The mechanism is that relevant literal imagery is shared by every competitor in the category, so it cannot differentiate. It crowds the design and limits the business if it diversifies. Distinctiveness, simplicity and memorability do the identifying work, and meaning is attached to the mark over time. [unsure]

After listing research's uses, Ogilvy admits research cannot tell you whether a truly new idea or product will succeed, because respondents cannot judge what they have never experienced, and it cannot write the ad or produce the big idea. On sample size, he says it should depend on the question and the precision it needs, not on a fixed rule. These limits are awkward for him because his doctrine rests on the big idea and on research-backed rules. The things research cannot validate are exactly the things he says matter most, so his central creative claims rest on judgment, not evidence. [unsure]

Freeman explains that an eyeline works because viewers instinctively follow where a person in the picture is looking. The gaze creates an implied line, a vector with direction, that carries attention across the frame to whatever is being looked at even though no line is drawn. When two eyelines converge, their meeting point becomes a strongly emphasised focus. The combined directional pull makes that spot the centre of attention and ties the figures together in a shared relationship, and it is one of the strongest implied-line effects.

The source's guidance runs the other way. The opening seconds are for Attract: hook the viewer with a strong, immersive opening and bring in the brand early. Direct asks for a clear call to action, with a visual CTA and voice-over and for action objectives a persistent or repeated on-screen prompt, but not as a replacement for the hook. So a CTA at two seconds, before any interest exists, is not what it recommends. Viewers need a reason before a request. The source gives no evidence for, or rule on, a CTA-first opening. [unsure]

The Law of the Word says a brand should own one word in the prospect's mind, because the mind simplifies and files each brand under a single concept. Trying for two dilutes both, so the brand ends up standing for nothing. The argument compares the brand's single slot in the mind with the multiple attributes a marketer wants to claim. Neither quantity is defined or measured. How many associations a mind holds is asserted, not shown, and strong brands plainly carry several associations. So the 'one word' limit is a metaphor presented as a mechanism. [unsure]

Pandey argues that the client is a partner, not an obstacle. Clients know their business and consumers, and good work comes from collaboration and trust. The mechanism is that clients who helped shape the work, and are challenged and respected in the process, champion it, run it longer and defend it internally, so ownership raises both quality and survival. The case is weakened because it rests on his long relationships with unusually supportive clients such as Pidilite and Cadbury. That is survivorship: he rarely reports approval processes that ruined work, and he does not separate the effect of a good client from the effect of collaboration. [unsure]

For awareness, the table prescribes roughly this. Attract: hook quickly with a tight, well-lit opening and a compelling story. Brand: show and say the brand and product early, within the first five seconds, and often, with audio mentions. Connect: human faces, emotion, humour or storytelling to make people feel something so the brand is remembered. Direct: a light touch, such as a soft CTA to watch, learn or visit, rather than hard conversion prompts. Brand prominence and recall carry the weight. [unsure]

Sullivan says you should argue for the work on strategy because creativity is subjective. If the debate is about whether the ad is clever or funny, it comes down to taste, and the client's taste wins. Strategy is objective ground both sides have already agreed on, so showing how the work delivers the approved strategy makes rejection harder to justify. His supporting fact is that clients are business people accountable for results and sales, not creative judges, and they are paying for a solution to a business problem.

The mechanism is that Indian consumers add new behaviours, products and values without discarding old ones. They combine tradition and modernity (both/and, not either/or), so change is accretion, not replacement. The framing is the national-character 'We are like that only' idea of Indian exceptionalism. The separation matters because the mechanism is testable and may apply to many transitional markets. It gives concrete predictions such as hybrid products, coexistence of channels and slower displacement. The essentialist framing is not testable and invites stereotyping, so you should carry the mechanism across, not the cultural claim.

Freeman gives two routes to duration in a still. One is a single long exposure, where movement records as blur or trails. The other is multiple or sequential exposures, several moments captured separately and then shown together. The merged version combines separate frames into one image, by multiple exposure or digital stacking, so several instants appear at once. It requires a fixed camera position with a static, registered background (a tripod, identical framing and exposure), so that only the moving subject changes between frames. [unsure]

Pandey largely places the problem outside advertising, in society and in the consumer realities ads reflect. Advertising mirrors the audience and cannot run far ahead of it. He adds that more women in creative roles and more sensitivity will help. What should be separated out is the empirical claim (ads reflect prevailing attitudes) from the normative excuse it provides (so advertisers bear limited responsibility). His reasoning treats reflection as exculpation, although ads also reinforce and shape norms. [unsure]

Samara says that without a consistent page grid, structure can live in the type system and other recurring cues. Examples are a limited, consistent set of typefaces, sizes and weights, a colour system, consistent image treatment, recurring elements such as folios, running heads and margins, and the rhythm and sequencing of spreads. The reader experiences unity through these consistent relationships and details even though each layout differs, so the structure is conceptual and typographic, not geometric.

Pandey found that Pidilite (Fevicol), which he saw as an unglamorous adhesives account, was one of the most creatively rewarding clients. Its founder, Balvant Parekh, and the team gave freedom, trusted humour and backed bold, earthy ideas, which produced the celebrated Fevicol campaigns. The episode establishes that a category's glamour does not determine creative opportunity, and that client attitude matters more. It is a single anecdote, told in hindsight by the account's beneficiary, so it does not establish that dull categories are generally better or reliably produce great work.

The book cautions against, first, building personas from assumptions instead of research, since invented personas turn into stereotypes that validate the team's biases. Second, it warns against loading them with irrelevant personal detail such as favourite foods, hobbies and names. What is wrong with such detail is that it has nothing to do with the goals and behaviours being designed for. It distracts critique and invites arguments about trivia, and it lends false precision that makes the persona feel real without making it useful for evaluating whether a design meets its objectives. [unsure]

SC 1.4.5 applies only if the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation. HTML and CSS generally can, so the event details should be provided as real text on the page, with the poster image added alongside or treated as supplementary. The poster also needs a text alternative under 1.1.1, but alt text does not satisfy 1.4.5. The CMS limitation is arguable at best, since the SC concerns the technology, not one tool. Putting the details in text also satisfies 1.4.9, which allows images of text only for pure decoration or where essential, provided the image is decorative or the information is duplicated. An image-only poster fails 1.4.9 outright.

Evaluations of the US National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign found the ads did not reduce drug use. Exposure was associated with increased intentions to use marijuana among teens. Berger's mechanism is social proof. By stressing how many young people use drugs, the ads signalled that drug use is common and normal, making the undesirable behaviour public. The research is Robert Hornik's (Annenberg School, University of Pennsylvania) and colleagues' evaluation of the campaign.

For Goodyear, Hopkins used the advertising itself to create dealer demand. Ads listed local dealers, or directed readers to named dealers, so consumers asked for the product at specific shops. Dealers qualified for a listing by stocking the product, carrying an agreed supply. It compounds because each listing sends customers into listed shops, which raises their turnover and draws more dealers wanting listings, which puts more stock on hand and makes the brand more available. No salesmen or discounts were needed. [unsure]

This is J.C. Penney under Ron Johnson, who scrapped coupons and sales for everyday fair pricing. Godin says customers were not buying low prices but the experience of the deal: the thrill of the hunt, the feeling of being a smart shopper, and the story they told themselves about winning. Removing the game removed what they valued, and sales collapsed. As evidence it is one well-known case explained in hindsight and confounded by other changes Johnson made at the same time (store redesign, brand mix, alienating core shoppers). It illustrates the point but does not isolate the cause.

Berger's routes are these. First, find inner remarkability by breaking a pattern and violating expectations. Something surprising in an ordinary category, like Snapple's cap facts or a hidden bar behind a hot-dog shop, exploits the attention and talk that surprise generates. Second, use game mechanics and insider status through scarcity and exclusivity, which exploit people's desire to look good, achieve status and be in the know. Both create social currency without a novel product feature. [unsure]

The caption is normal-size text (11pt is below 18pt/14pt bold), so SC 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1, and 4.6:1 passes on the numbers. The Understanding documents note that very thin or decorative fonts are harder to read and that stroke width affects legibility. They advise authors to use higher contrast for thin fonts, but the contrast calculation does not account for font weight. So the source acknowledges the problem and encourages more contrast, but stops short of making it a failure. Technically the caption conforms.

Freeman uses an abalone shell as a background behind a quartz crystal, chosen for its iridescent colour and texture rather than for any contextual connection. The shell complements and sets off the crystal's clarity and form. The general permission is that in still life and constructed images the photographer may choose backgrounds and props purely for their graphic and aesthetic contribution, such as colour, tone and contrast, without needing a logical or natural relationship to the subject. [unsure]

The re-release material shows posters being redesigned for new circulation. Distributors update imagery to the later status of stars and to current graphic fashion, and emphasise what has since become famous about the film rather than reproducing the original. That suggests leaning on the elements the later following cherishes. It does not settle whether to preserve the original visual identity for nostalgia or modernise it. What you would need to know, and the source cannot tell you, is who the following is, what they value (iconic scenes, stars, the original poster art), and how the new audience's expectations differ. That requires current audience research. [unsure]

One sign of a platform-sized idea is that executions come easily. Many different ads and media extensions suggest themselves, and it can run for years. The other is that other people, colleagues and clients, start adding their own executions and building on it. Distrust the first most, because ease of generating executions can come from a format or formula (a template or gimmick) rather than a genuine idea. Many executions can simply be repetition. The test is whether the idea stays fresh and meaningful across executions. [unsure]

Instead of evening out tones, Freeman increased contrast and pushed the tonal separation so that the vertical lines of the planking became the dominant graphic feature. He went for a strong, almost abstract rhythm of lines, not a balanced full-range rendering. He also removed colour, converting to black and white or strongly desaturating, and cropped out distracting elements, so nothing competed with the linear pattern. [unsure]

The form is the song-and-dance sequence (film music and song picturisation), which the authors call the most distinctive element of Hindi cinema but do not study in depth. The book is about visual culture: sets, costumes, posters and publicity. Songs are a musical and performative form outside that scope and would need a separate study. As a result, every claim about Hindi cinema as a whole is partial. The book describes the medium with its defining component largely left out, so its generalisations apply to the visual and material culture of the films, not to the medium entire. [unsure]

The second failure is being too fast, meaning too obvious. The fuse is so short the reader gets it instantly with no effort and no small pleasure of working it out. Sullivan says this is a failure because an ad that explains itself completely leaves the reader nothing to do. There is no reward and no engagement, so it is not memorable or persuasive. A slight delay, where the reader completes the idea, creates the 'aha' that makes the ad stick. Too slow and they give up. Too fast and they don't care.

Godin's method: choose two axes that matter to the people you serve, such as price, speed, convenience, exclusivity, efficacy, sustainability or ease of use. Plot the alternatives on the XY grid, then pick a spot at the edge, an empty extreme where you stand for something specific and different. The trade-off is that choosing axes means giving up everything else, and you must choose what your target customers actually care about. If you choose axes that matter only to you, or that customers cannot perceive, you occupy an empty corner nobody wants. The customer sees no difference, has no reason to choose you and falls back on price.

Jain argues that condemning or banning an image acknowledges and amplifies its power. Controversy increases its circulation, visibility and symbolic charge, and turns it into a rallying point that mobilises communities around it, so the attack confirms the image's efficacy. She recommends paying attention to how images actually circulate and work in their contexts of use, including devotional, commercial and political ones. Rather than moral condemnation, which feeds the image, she calls for understanding the social and economic networks that give the image its force. [unsure]

A complex surface is one that produces more than one kind of reflection at once: diffuse, direct (specular) and often polarised reflection. Examples are varnished wood, glossy paint over texture, or leather with a sheen. Each reflection type behaves differently. Diffuse reflection appears from any light angle, while direct reflection appears only when the light lies within the family of angles. Adding more light cannot control them separately. You must decide how much of each reflection you want and manage them independently, placing sources inside or outside the family of angles, using polarisers, and lighting parts of the subject separately. [unsure]

The source argues celebrities are often chosen for reasons internal to the client or agency, not effectiveness. Clients enjoy association with stars and want to meet them. A celebrity is a safe, defensible choice that sells the campaign internally, and a star is a shortcut when there is no idea. None of these reasons concern whether the ad persuades consumers. The general hazard is decisions driven by the decision-makers' own incentives and gratification rather than the audience, a principal-agent or proxy problem, which leads to vampire effects where the star overshadows the brand. [unsure]

Ogilvy claims that conventional ad graphics, such as headline above the picture, display typefaces, reversed type, fancy borders and a look unlike the surrounding editorial, signal 'this is an advertisement' at a glance, before any word is read, and readers skip it. He proposes making ads look editorial: layouts like magazine or newspaper pages, a photograph with a caption beneath, the headline below the picture, serif body type in black on white, and a news-like style, because people read editorial more than ads.

The book ends by noting that the visual culture it describes belongs to a period that is ending or has ended. Hindi cinema was being transformed by globalisation, the rise of 'Bollywood', multiplexes, new technologies such as digital production and publicity, corporate financing, and changing audiences and diaspora markets. Hand-painted posters and older forms were giving way. The reader therefore has to treat the rest of the book as historical, describing a particular era, and check every generalisation against later practice rather than applying it to contemporary Indian cinema. [unsure]

Berger's habitat is the set of cues in the environment that trigger thoughts of a product. What matters is how often those triggers occur and how strongly they are linked to it, so a product with a frequent trigger stays top of mind. His evidence that a habitat can be grown is Kit Kat's 'a break's best friend' campaign linking Kit Kat with coffee. Coffee is a frequent trigger, and the campaign reportedly lifted sales. The reported effect applies to the people exposed to the campaign, in the market and period studied, not to consumers generally, and it is a correlational market result, not a controlled test. [unsure]

A system trained on naturalist photography would by default violate the conventions of bazaar devotional images. Those images use frontality (the deity faces and meets the viewer's gaze for darshan), iconographic correctness (attributes, mudras, vahanas, colour codes), flat and saturated colour, idealised bodies, auspicious symmetry and a centralised composition rather than candid naturalistic perspective. Frontality, gaze direction, symmetry and required attributes can be checked. Sacrality, efficacy and devotional appropriateness cannot. Nobody should build a fixed essentialist rulebook of 'authentic Indian taste' from this ethnographic material, or tools that mass-produce sacred images in ways communities might find offensive. [unsure]

On Jain's account of the bazaar's commercial networks, a corporate-gifting catalogue's sales measure the choices of intermediaries: corporate purchasers buying gifts that are safe, auspicious, inoffensive and suitable for giving. They reflect that particular channel's economics (price points, supply, what distributors stocked), not what end viewers or devotees prefer, use or venerate. So the ranking measures gift-market fit in one circulation channel, shaped by supply, and says little about aesthetic or devotional value or demand elsewhere.

Ogilvy praises Procter & Gamble's disciplined consistency: sticking with proven formulas, the same positioning for decades, rigorous testing and never chopping and changing. Then he names that same consistency as its weakness. The formula-bound ads became predictable and dull, and it was hard to break into fresh creative territory. The double reading qualifies his own doctrine that you should stick with a campaign and build a consistent brand image. Consistency of positioning is a virtue, but consistency of formula and execution can harden into stale sameness. [unsure]

The objections are: (1) noise reduction is costly; (2) rules and algorithms can introduce their own errors and bias; (3) mechanical rules deny dignity, since people want to be judged as individuals and heard; (4) rigid rules freeze values that should evolve; (5) clear rules invite gaming; (6) some unpredictability deters wrongdoing; (7) rules demoralise judges and stifle creativity. The structural reply is that these objections target particular crude methods, not noise reduction itself. The costs of noise must be weighed against the costs of reducing it, and the right mix of decision hygiene, rules and standards can usually keep most of the benefit while answering the objection. [unsure]

Bijapurkar distinguishes molting, where a consumer sheds an old skin and replaces old behaviours with new ones, from morphing, where the consumer gradually transforms, keeping the old and adding the new so the underlying identity persists. Indian consumer change is mostly morphing. The detection problem is that surveys and trackers keep finding continuity in the old behaviours and miss that people are becoming something different, or they mistake additions for replacement. The evidence is mostly her consulting observations and illustrative examples, plus some macro consumption data, not systematic longitudinal studies. [unsure]

Airey suggests that if you cannot explain your design rationale clearly and simply in words, the design may not be resolved. Writing the rationale tests the concept. The claim is that a clear idea can be put in clear prose. The implication only runs one way. Muddled writing may indicate a muddled design, but an articulate rationale does not prove the logo is good, since plausible stories can be written for weak marks after the fact. The test catches some failures and certifies none. [unsure]

Hopkins objects that people of limited means do not want reminders of their poverty. Economy and saving appeals point to what they lack and carry the stigma of cheapness. He substitutes positive appeals to pleasure, aspiration, quality, health or beauty, offering what they want to become rather than what they save. His evidence is anecdotal and experiential: campaigns he ran or tested where the aspirational appeal outsold the economy appeal. These are keyed-return comparisons within his own practice, not controlled studies, and are reported from memory. [unsure]

The contrast ratio uses relative luminance only because luminance contrast is what matters for legibility and is perceived by nearly everyone, including people with colour-vision deficiencies. Hue differences may be invisible to people with colour blindness, so they cannot be relied on. The source notes the reasoning breaks down for red with protanopia. People with protan deficiency perceive red as much darker than its computed luminance suggests, so red on dark (or red-dependent) combinations can have less effective contrast than the formula reports. [unsure]

The five-second criterion, that an idea must grab and be understood within a few seconds, comes from Pandey's practitioner rhetoric and anecdotes, not measurement. The record should treat it as a heuristic with no validated threshold, no definition of what counts as grabbing attention, no measurement procedure and no evidence linking it to effectiveness. So it should be noted as a directional principle, not adopted as a pass mark. Turning it into a scored threshold would give false precision to a rule of thumb. [unsure]

The song sequence is licensed to suspend narrative time and linear progression, spatial continuity and realism (sudden jumps to foreign or fantasy locations), diegetic logic (characters burst into song and dance), costume continuity (multiple changes within one song), and social and moral constraints, allowing romance, eroticism and desire shown more openly than in the narrative. So you cannot read a film's story directly from its songs. They are semi-autonomous spaces of fantasy and spectacle that often express what the narrative cannot, and they circulate separately, so treating them as plot summaries misreads both.

For twelve images made as one body of work, Carroll's principle about series applies. Judge the images as a set: coherence, consistency of approach and theme, sequencing, and whether each picture contributes to the whole. Weaker individual images may earn a place if they serve the narrative, and strong images that don't fit should go. The single-image principle, that each photo must stand on its own and be judged in isolation, gets this wrong. It would pick the individually strongest images even if they don't hang together and would cut connective images the series needs. [unsure]

Berger's trade-off is between how often a trigger occurs and how strongly it is linked to your product. A very frequent, generic cue like red is already associated with many things, so any one link is weak and diluted, much like trying to be heard in a crowded room of competing associations. The link must be distinctive to work. To resolve it, choose a cue that is frequent in the target audience's environment but not already heavily linked to other things, and build a strong, specific connection to it, as Kit Kat did with coffee. [unsure]
